claims.text: High-entropy mixing in noble-metal nanocatalysts generates local lattice distortions.
Local lattice distortions equalize the atomic mobilities of the constituent noble metals.
Balanced interdiffusion leads to uniform, single-phase alloy formation.
Uniform single-phase formation produces well-dispersed active surface sites.
Well-dispersed active sites improve catalytic performance relative to alloys having imbalanced diffusion kinetics.
The initial material is a nanostructured, incompletely alloyed mixture of Au, Pt, Pd, or Ag precursors with spatially varying local composition.
Controlled thermal annealing promotes interdiffusion and alloy homogenization while preserving nanoscale features.
An annealing-temperature window exists in which atomic diffusion is sufficient but agglomeration and sintering are avoided.
Chemical disparity in a high-entropy mixture creates a rough atomic-scale energy landscape.
The rough energy landscape reduces mobility differences among constituent atoms during annealing.
Reduced mobility differences promote uniform intermixing and prevent phase separation.
Similar atomic mobilities in refractory high-entropy alloys support defect recombination and homogeneous microstructures.
Relative to a conventional or binary noble-metal alloy, the high-entropy nanocatalyst will have a more homogeneous single-phase microstructure detectable by XRD and TEM.
Relative to the baseline alloy, the high-entropy nanocatalyst will exhibit higher and more stable catalytic turnover frequency under identical conditions.
The mechanism should hold when the selected noble metals have relatively similar atomic sizes and electronic characteristics.
The mechanism should hold only at temperatures that permit diffusion without causing sintering or phase agglomeration.
Analogous defect-recombination behavior has been observed in refractory high-entropy alloys under irradiation.
Greater measured interdiffusion or structural homogeneity should correlate with improved catalytic performance across annealing conditions.
